headline: The Catch Behind Robinhood's Cheap Margin
lede: A screenshot of a Robinhood Gold account disclosing borrowing capacity of over a million dollars at 4.25% has prompted a simple question: is this actually a good deal? The answer depends heavily on where you sit in the rate table — and what you're willing to ignore in the fine print.
body:
Robinhood's margin rates look attractive against the industry's worst offenders. At the $1 million-to-$10 million tier — the rate that caught this account holder's eye — Robinhood charges 4.25% annually. That is genuinely competitive against Charles Schwab and Fidelity, whose base rates sit near 10.575%, a relic of the era when large brokerages treated margin interest as a reliable profit center requiring little justification. The comparison flatters Robinhood substantially: borrowing $1 million at Schwab costs roughly $100,000 per year in interest; at Robinhood's published rate, that same loan costs $42,500.

But the honest benchmark is not Schwab. Interactive Brokers, the brokerage preferred by professional traders and sophisticated retail investors, prices margin loans at its benchmark rate — effectively tracking the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, currently near 3.63% — plus a spread of roughly 1.5% for smaller balances and as little as 0.5% for larger ones. For the retail investor borrowing $1 million, IBKR Pro's all-in rate has historically landed somewhere in the 5.1%–5.8% range depending on tier blending, though IBKR's benchmark-linked pricing means its effective rate moves with monetary policy in near real time. SOFR is the overnight rate at which large financial institutions lend each other cash secured by U.S. Treasury collateral; it replaced LIBOR as the dominant short-term dollar benchmark. Robinhood's published rates, by contrast, are fixed tiers not mechanically tied to any benchmark, which means they can lag Fed cuts — or stay elevated when rates fall.

The $1,000 interest-free hook deserves particular scrutiny. Robinhood Gold costs $5 per month, or $60 annually. At the sub-$50,000 rate of 5%, the interest-free $1,000 allowance saves $50 per year in forgone interest — less than the subscription fee itself. The promotion is best understood as a loss leader that nudges retail customers toward margin habits. For accounts small enough to borrow in the sub-$50,000 tier at 5%, the call money rate — the rate at which banks lend funds to brokerages for the purpose of financing margin loans to customers — is a useful yardstick: call money tracked roughly 4.3%–4.5% during much of 2025 and early 2026, meaning Robinhood's 5% rate at the lowest tier captures a spread above its own cost of funds.

Then there is hypothecation. A margin account gives the broker the legal right to pledge your securities as collateral for its own borrowings — this is standard across all brokerages. But Robinhood also operates a fully paid securities lending program through which it lends out shares in cash accounts that have opted in, keeping a portion of the lending revenue. Under its customer agreement (revised April 2026), loaned securities are explicitly excluded from Securities Investor Protection Corporation coverage; the collateral held at a third-party bank constitutes the lender's principal recourse if Robinhood fails to return shares. This is not unique to Robinhood, but it is worth understanding before treating the account as equivalent to a custodied brokerage relationship. Hypothecation is the pledging of securities as collateral without transferring title; rehypothecation goes further, allowing the pledgee to re-pledge those same securities to a third party.

The math on the implied yield arbitrage — borrow at 4.25%, invest in an S&P 500 index fund yielding more — is less elegant than it first appears. The S&P 500's trailing earnings yield stood near 3.84% as of early May 2026, below the proposed borrowing rate. Forward estimates pencil out closer to 4.1%, which narrows the theoretical spread to roughly 15 basis points before frictions. A basis point is one-hundredth of one percentage point. Margin interest paid on loans used to purchase taxable investments is deductible against net investment income under U.S. tax law, which improves the after-tax cost of the loan for itemizers — but the deduction is capped at net investment income and provides no benefit in years of capital losses. More critically, the calculation assumes an equity portfolio that rises smoothly; the actual risk is the forced liquidation that occurs if the portfolio falls 25–30% and the broker issues a margin call. During the 2022 bear market and the 2025 tariff-shock volatility, brokers liquidated positions at distressed prices across thousands of accounts, often without prior notice. Robinhood has historically been more aggressive than full-service brokers in triggering automatic liquidations.

For the account holder who genuinely has $1 million in securities and wants cheap leverage, the honest advice is straightforward: the rate is competitive versus the incumbents, but Interactive Brokers offers a structurally cheaper product for active traders, and a securities-backed line of credit from a private bank may be cheaper still for buy-and-hold investors with concentrated positions. The real catches are not the rate itself but the platform risk during volatility, the hypothecation exposure, and the optical generosity of the $1,000 interest-free tranche — a figure that means something to a $50,000 account but rounds to a rounding error on $1 million.

concepts.definition: A loan from a brokerage collateralized by securities held in the customer's account, allowing the investor to buy more assets than cash on hand would permit. The broker can demand repayment or sell collateral if the account value falls below a required threshold.

The pledging of securities as collateral for a loan without transferring legal ownership. In a margin account, the broker holds the right to re-pledge (rehypothecate) those securities to its own creditors, which can complicate recovery if the broker fails.

Secured Overnight Financing Rate — the overnight interest rate at which large financial institutions lend each other cash backed by U.S. Treasury collateral. It replaced LIBOR in 2023 as the dominant short-term dollar benchmark and is published daily by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

The interest rate banks charge brokerages on overnight loans used to fund customers' margin accounts. It is typically close to the federal funds rate and sets the floor for the cost at which brokerages can themselves borrow the money they re-lend to margin customers.

fact_check: IBKR Pro USD margin rates are benchmark-linked (tracking SOFR at ~3.63% as of May 2026) plus spreads of 0.5%–1.5% depending on tier, producing all-in rates roughly in the 5.1%–5.8% range for mid-size balances — materially higher than Robinhood's published 4.25% tier for $1M–$10M balances. Robinhood's rate advantage at the $1M+ tier is therefore genuine against IBKR, though IBKR's benchmark-linked pricing falls automatically when the Fed cuts rates, while Robinhood's tiers are discretionary. Schwab and Fidelity base rates near 10.575% make both IBKR and Robinhood look cheap by comparison.
